 Social Security’s Death Benefit Is $255. Congress Capped It in 1954, When It Covered Much of a Funeral, and Has Never Raised It Since
 Vilma Rios Wed, November 18, 2026 at 4:52 AM CST 6 min read Quick Read 
 Social Security's $255 death payment has stayed frozen since 1954; had it tracked the taxable wage base, it would be worth about $13,000 today. 
 Only a spouse in the household, a spouse eligible for survivor benefits, or an eligible child can claim it, and divorced spouses get nothing. 
 The average aged widow's monthly check is about $1,919 after the 2026 COLA, dwarfing the lump sum, so survivors should call SSA early.

 When a worker covered by Social Security dies, the government sends the surviving spouse a one-time payment of $255.00. Congress limited that amount in 1954. More than 70 years of inflation, wage growth and cost-of-living raises have passed since then, and the amount hasn't changed. 
 fizkes / Shutterstock.com The payment is called the lump-sum death payment , and it comes from Section 202(i) of the Social Security Act. Below: what the payment is worth today, who can claim it, how the IRS handles it, and why the monthly survivor check matters far more. 
 How the 1954 Lump-Sum Death Payment Cap Became Permanent 
 The lump sum is older than monthly survivor benefits. The Congressional Research Service (CRS) says it was the only benefit available to survivors of insured workers who died before age 65 between 1937 and 1939. At that time it equaled 3.5% of the worker's covered earnings. 
 The money once covered real expenses. CRS notes that before 1952, $255 was more than three times the maximum monthly Social Security benefit. After the 1954 cap, CRS says, almost all payments have equaled $255 since 1982. 
 Congress later tightened eligibility as well. SSA's operations manual references the 1981 budget law, Public Law 97-35. CRS reports that in the majority of deaths, no payment is made.

 What $255 Would Be Worth If It Had Kept Up With Wages 
 Story Continues The taxable wage base makes a useful benchmark because it rises with wages every year. In 1954, Social Security taxed earnings up to $3,600, so $255 equaled about 7.1% of a top earner's taxable pay.

 The 2026 wage base is 51.25 times the 1954 figure. If the death payment had grown by the same multiple, it would be about $13,069. 
 Cost-of-living adjustments don't touch it either. Monthly benefits rose 2.8% for 2026, and the 2027 COLA is 3.6%. A 3.6% raise would lift the death payment to $264.18, but the law sets it as a flat dollar amount, so it remains at $255. 
 The program costs very little. In 2023, SSA made the payment for about 841,961 deaths, totaling about $215 million. That's roughly 0.02% of all Social Security benefit payments. 
 Who Can Claim the $255 Death Benefit, and the Two-Year Filing Deadline 
 SSA pays the lump sum to the first eligible person in this order, per its operations manual: 
 A surviving spouse living in the same household at the time of death. 
 A surviving spouse eligible for or entitled to widow(er)'s, mother's or father's benefits on the worker's record in the month of death. 
 A child eligible for or entitled to benefits on the worker's record in the month of death. 
 The worker must have been fully or currently insured. A surviving divorced spouse is not entitled to receive the LSDP, even one who collects monthly benefits. If an application is required, it must be filed within 2 years after the NH's death, although SSA can extend that deadline for good cause. Grown children who pay for a parent's funeral usually get nothing. 
 IRS Rules Make the Death Payment Tax-Free 
 According to IRS Publication 915, the lump-sum death payment "isn't subject to tax." Publication 525 puts it next to SSI as income that isn't subject to federal income tax. On Form SSA-1099 it appears as a nontaxable payment and is subtracted out before net benefits are reported. 
 Publication 915 also says not to confuse it with a retroactive lump sum of back benefits. Back benefits can be taxable, and you may be able to reduce that tax with a special election under 26 U.S.C. § 86(e). 
 Monthly survivor checks get different treatment. Under Section 86, up to 50% of benefits can become taxable once provisional income passes a base amount, and up to 85% once it passes $44,000 on a joint return or $34,000 for a single filer. That base is $32,000 on a joint return and $25,000 for a single filer (26 U.S.C. § 86(c)(1)). The law sets these as flat dollar amounts with no inflation adjustment, which makes them a second fixed number. Once a widow starts filing as single, her threshold falls, so the same income can leave more of her benefits taxable. 
 Why the Monthly Survivor Check Matters More Than $255 
 After the 2026 COLA, the estimated average benefit for an aged widow(er) is $1,919 a month. When you call SSA about the $255, the agency also starts the claim for that much larger monthly benefit, so make the call early. 
 Some changes are coming. The Social Security Survivor Benefits Equity Act has been introduced in the 119th Congress as S.3357 and H.R.6424. It would raise the lump sum and index it to inflation. An earlier version would have paid $2,900, but none of these proposals has become law. Funding is another obstacle: the 2026 Trustees Report projects that the retirement and survivors trust fund will run out in late 2032, after which incoming revenue would cover 78% of scheduled benefits. 
 A widow's switch to single filing status and when to claim survivor benefits are worth working through with a qualified tax or financial professional (we also put the survivor benefit math into a free one-page guide, here).
